newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi paves way for return of exiled royal.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi paves way for return of exiled royal.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Wednesday took a first step towards allowing the son of Italy's last king to come home, 50 years after the monarchy was abolished and all male descendants barred entry.

The centre-left cabinet approved Prodi's proposal for a draft law to allow Vittorio Emanuele, who currently lives in exile in Switzerland, and all other male heirs of the House of Savoy to return to Italy.
The draft, which will be drawn up at a future cabinet meeting, must be passed by both Italian houses of parliament before it can become law.
"It seems the right thing to do," Prodi told reporters.
"It was something that needed to be done," said Deputy Prime Minister Walter Veltroni. "It's been talked about for such a long time."
The opposition hard-right National Alliance and the Monarchist Party welcomed the move.

But the hard-left Communist Refoundation party, which secures Prodi's parliamentary majority, said the Savoy dynasty could not be so easily forgiven for its complicity with over 20 years of fascist rule under dictator Benito Mussolini.
"As long as the dynasty remains, there also remains their gigantic responsibility for the fascist regime," Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti told reporters.

Vittorio Emanuele's father, King Umberto II, was forced into exile when war-weary Italians voted to scrap the monarchy on June 2, 1946, blaming their royal family for allowing the fascist dictatorship to take root.

Veltroni denied suggestions that Wednesday's move was intended to appease right-wing voters. But Bertinotti criticised the government for timing the announcement ahead of International Labour Day on Thursday.
"The government would have done well to give a sign of solidarity to Italy's workers," he said.

Vittorio Emanuele, who left Italy aged nine, said last year he would like to return to Rome and work as a special foreign affairs ambassador, but added he had no political ambitions and wanted to be "an ordinary Italian".
Many Italians, including President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro and his predecessors as head of state, have called on the country to forget the past and change the 1946 law.

The House of Savoy united Italy when Vittorio Emanuele I of Piedmont became the country's first king in 1861. The former royal palace atop Rome's Quirinale hill is now the president's official residence.
